summary: IGP Flexible Algorithm computes constrained paths using administrative policy. This document adds an extension that includes or excludes links based on reverse affinity, using link attributes seen from the opposite direction. It updates RFC 9350 and RFC 9843.

plainLanguage.summary: A link between two routers can be marked differently in each direction, and a fault such as a failing cable is usually noticed by the router at the receiving end. This document lets a path calculation look at the marking on the link in the direction opposite to the one being travelled, so that a fault seen at one end can keep traffic away from the link altogether.

subtitle: Lets Flex-Algorithm prune links using the Admin Groups set on the reverse direction of a link.

tldr.problem: An IGP Flexible Algorithm can exclude links from a path by checking attributes set on the link in the direction of travel. Some link faults are only visible at the far end of a link, so the far end marks the link, but the far end can only mark the direction pointing back at itself.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9917 adds three rules to the Flex-Algorithm path computation that look at the Extended Administrative Groups of the reverse direction of a link: exclude, include-any and include-all. The rules are carried in new sub-TLVs inside the Flexible Algorithm Definition, with type 10, 11 and 12 for both IS-IS and OSPF.
tldr.outcome: The document updates RFC 9350 and RFC 9843, and creates an IANA registry that holds the ordered set of Flex-Algorithm pruning rules, so that later extensions can add their own without renumbering the existing ones.

today: RFC 9917 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 9350 and RFC 9843, registers three new sub-TLV types for both IS-IS and OSPF, and creates the IGP Flex-Algorithm Path Computation Rules registry at IANA, whose initial contents list this document's three rules as numbers 8, 9 and 10.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IGP protocols historically computed the best paths over the network solely based on the IGP metric assigned to the links. An IGP Flex-Algorithm, as specified in RFC 9350, allows IGPs to compute constraint-based paths. Several mechanisms to include or exclude a link during the Flex-Algorithm path calculation have already been defined: link inclusion or exclusion based on the presence of specific Admin Groups, link exclusion based on the presence of a specific Shared Risk Link Group, link exclusion based on minimum bandwidth, and link exclusion based on maximum delay.

This document extends IGP Flex-Algorithm with additional constraints for inclusion or exclusion of links in the path, based on Admin Groups associated with the reverse direction of the shortest path first computation.

The document updates RFC 9350 and RFC 9843 by creating a new IANA registry that specifies the ordered set of rules used to prune links from the topology during the Flex-Algorithm path computation. The term OSPF in this document covers both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: A Flex-Algorithm is a named set of rules that an interior routing protocol uses to pick a path for traffic of a particular kind. Some of those rules keep a link out of the path when the link carries a certain mark. This document adds rules that look at the mark on the link in the opposite direction, so that a problem reported by one router can keep traffic away from the link in both directions.

sections.title: Use Case Example
sections.content:
The Flexible Algorithm Definition can specify Extended Administrative Groups that the operator uses to include or exclude links during the Flex-Algorithm path computation. These link Extended Administrative Groups are checked in the path direction of the computation, for example in the direction from the root vertex towards vertices of increasing distance.

In certain scenarios it is beneficial to evaluate the Extended Administrative Groups associated with the reverse direction of a link, rather than solely those in the direction of path computation. Consider a point-to-point link represented as a pair of directed edges between two nodes, A and B. When computing a path from A to B, issues such as input errors on the link, detectable only at the receiving node B, may be operationally significant. An operator might monitor metrics like Cyclic Redundancy Check errors or other input-related faults at node B and apply thresholds over a defined observation period. If such a threshold is exceeded, node B may locally assign specific Extended Administrative Groups to the link in the direction from B to A.

To accommodate this operational intent, the Flex-Algorithm can be extended to inspect the Extended Administrative Groups of the reverse-direction edge when evaluating the forward-direction edge during path computation. This enables the exclusion of links from the computed topology based on conditions detected at the far end of the link, improving network reliability and policy control.
sections.plainLanguage: Take two routers joined by a link. The link is really two one-way edges, and each can carry its own marks. Errors on the link are noticed by the router that receives the traffic, so the router at the far end is the one that can see them and act on them. It can mark the edge pointing back towards its own side, but it cannot mark the edge in the direction the traffic is going, because that mark would have to come from the other router. This document lets the path calculation read the mark on the far end's edge and act on it.

sections.title: Deployment Consideration
sections.content:
Threshold-based setting of the link Extended Administrative Groups must be done with care, to avoid excessive flooding and constant Flex-Algorithm path recalculation.

One possible approach is to use two different thresholds when setting and unsetting the Extended Administrative Group on the link. For example, when setting the Extended Administrative Group on the link based on the percentage of certain incoming errors, a higher threshold is used for setting and a lower threshold for unsetting the group.

Many implementations provide a throttling mechanism that limits the rate at which the Link State PDU in the case of IS-IS, or the Link State Advertisement in the case of OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, is updated at the originator. Such a mechanism is typically not specific to any particular link attribute, but considers any change in the PDU or advertisement. Applying such a throttling mechanism can also avoid frequent changes in the setting of the Extended Administrative Group on a link affecting the stability of the receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the mark is advertised to the whole network, a mark that flickers on and off will cause a storm of updates and make every router recompute its paths. Two habits help. Use a higher threshold to set the mark than to clear it, so that a fault near the threshold does not flap. And use the throttling that routers already have for link state updates, so that repeated changes are sent out at a steady rate rather than all at once.

sections.title: The Reverse Admin Group Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Exclude Reverse Admin Group Sub-TLV advertises the exclude rule used during the Flex-Algorithm path calculation. It is a sub-TLV of the IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Definition Sub-TLV, with a one-octet Type field whose value is 10, a one-octet Length field that is variable and dependent on the size of the Extended Admin Group, and the Extended Administrative Group value itself. The length must be a multiple of 4 octets; if it is not, the entire sub-TLV must be ignored by the receiver.

The sub-TLV must not appear more than once in a single IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Definition Sub-TLV, and if it does, that Definition Sub-TLV must be ignored. It must also not appear more than once in the set of Definition Sub-TLVs for a given Flex-Algorithm from a given IS; if it does, the sub-TLV in the first occurrence in the lowest-numbered Link State PDU from that IS is used and the others are ignored.

The IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Include-Any Reverse Admin Group Sub-TLV has an identical format, with the type value 11, and the same occurrence rules. The IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Include-All Reverse Admin Group Sub-TLV has an identical format, with the type value 12, and the same occurrence rules.

The OSPF equivalents follow the same pattern inside the OSPF Flexible Algorithm Definition TLV. The OSPF Flexible Algorithm Exclude Reverse Admin Group Sub-TLV has a two-octet Type field with the value 10 and a two-octet Length field with the same multiple-of-4 requirement; the include-any and include-all sub-TLVs have type values 11 and 12. The OSPF occurrence rules are the same, except that the sub-TLV must not appear more than once in a given OSPF Flexible Algorithm Definition TLV, and if it does, that TLV must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule travels in its own small record inside the record that defines the Flex-Algorithm. The IS-IS version numbers its records with one byte and the OSPF version with two, and the numbers are 10 for exclude, 11 for include-any and 12 for include-all. The length of the record must be a multiple of four bytes, because the group value it carries is made of four-byte groups. A record that is duplicated makes the whole definition unusable, so a router ignores it rather than guess.

sections.title: Path Calculation
sections.content:
The procedures augment the rules defined in Section 13 of RFC 9350 by introducing additional constraints based on Administrative Groups associated with the reverse direction of a link.

First, check whether any exclude reverse Admin Group rule is part of the Flex-Algorithm definition. If such a rule exists, check whether any Admin Group that is part of the exclude rule is also set on the link in the reverse direction. If such an Admin Group is set on the link in the reverse direction, the link must be pruned from the computation.

Second, check whether any include-any reverse Admin Group rule is part of the Flex-Algorithm definition. If such a rule exists, check whether any Admin Group that is part of the include-any rule is also set on the link in the reverse direction. If no such Admin Group is set on the link in the reverse direction, the link must be pruned from the computation.

Third, check whether any include-all reverse Admin Group rule is part of the Flex-Algorithm definition. If such a rule exists, check whether all Admin Groups that are part of the include-all rule are also set on the link in the reverse direction. If all such Admin Groups are not set on the link in the reverse direction, the link must be pruned from the computation.
sections.plainLanguage: Three rules run during the calculation, and each one can remove a link. The exclude rule removes the link if the reverse direction carries any of the listed marks. The include-any rule removes the link if the reverse direction carries none of them. The include-all rule removes the link unless the reverse direction carries every one of them. In each case the mark that matters is the one on the link pointing the other way.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has registered types 10, 11 and 12 in the IS-IS Sub-Sub-TLVs for Flexible Algorithm Definition Sub-TLV registry under the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry group, for the exclude, include-any and include-all reverse Admin Group sub-TLVs. The same three types have been registered in the OSPF Flexible Algorithm Definition TLV Sub-TLVs registry under the Open Shortest Path First Parameters registry group.

IANA has created a new registry called IGP Flex-Algorithm Path Computation Rules within the Interior Gateway Protocol Parameters registry group, with a registration procedure of Expert Review. The registry specifies the ordered set of rules used to prune links from the topology during the Flex-Algorithm path computation, and there is no upper bound on the number of rules it supports. The initial entries are the ten rules that exist today, and this document's three reverse Admin Group rules are numbers 8, 9 and 10.

The guidance for the designated expert says that when a new constraint is defined, the rule associated with it may be inserted at any position, because backwards compatibility is guaranteed by nodes not taking part in an algorithm whose definition specifies a constraint they do not support. The relative ordering of the existing rules must not be altered, because doing so has the potential to create backwards compatibility issues. Rules must not be deleted, because they are only used conditionally on the information carried in the winning definition. Rules must not be merged or repeated.
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers the new record types for both protocols, and it creates a list of all the pruning rules in the order they are applied. That list matters because the rules can be added by later documents without disturbing the ones already there: a new rule can go anywhere in the list, the existing order must not be changed, and nothing is ever removed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document inherits the security considerations of RFC 9350. It adds no new mechanisms of its own, and the new sub-TLVs carry only administrative group values, which are the same kind of link attribute that the existing Flex-Algorithm sub-TLVs already carry.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security considerations of its own and follows the rules already set for Flex-Algorithm. The new records carry only the same kind of link attribute that the existing ones carry, so they do not open anything new.

items.text: The link between A and B is a pair of directed edges, and each can carry its own administrative groups.

items.title: Errors are seen at the far end
items.text: Input errors on the link are detected by the node that receives the traffic, at node B.

items.title: The far end marks the other edge
items.text: Node B can set administrative groups on the edge pointing back from B to A.

items.title: The calculation looks backwards
items.text: The new rules let the path computation act on the forward link because of what the reverse edge says.
